questions.scenario: A logistics partner asks for "AI that handles our carrier claims". Claims require reading carrier letters, checking contract rates in an existing rate engine, calculating refund amounts, and approving payouts above $5,000.
questions.question: Which decomposition is most appropriate?

answer_options.A: Claude reads letters, looks up contract rates from what it knows, calculates refunds, and approves all payouts.
answer_options.B: Claude handles every step end to end, with a human spot-checking 5% of outputs each week.
answer_options.C: The rate engine handles everything, and Claude only formats the final notification email to the carrier.
answer_options.D: Claude extracts and drafts; the rate engine calculates; humans approve payouts over $5,000.

questions.explanation: Correct. Each part goes to the owner that fits: language to Claude, authoritative data to systems, high-stakes approval to humans.

option_explanations.A: Over-assigning to Claude: rates are authoritative values, and arithmetic and approvals need deterministic systems or humans.
option_explanations.B: Sampling doesn't fit high-value, hard-to-reverse payouts.
option_explanations.C: Under-uses Claude for the language work (reading varied letters) it does well.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Each part goes to the owner that fits: language to Claude, authoritative data to systems, high-stakes approval to humans.

questions.exam_lesson: Split work into Claude, existing systems and humans before choosing a pattern.
questions.source_reference: M1 Decomposition; M1 four properties

questions.scenario: A sponsor watched a working demo of a contract-flagging assistant and asks the architect to confirm feasibility today. Volume, contract lengths and response-time needs haven't been discussed.
questions.question: What should the architect do next?

answer_options.A: Confirm feasibility now, because the working demo already proves the model has the capability.
answer_options.B: Gather volume, input-size and latency needs, then give a verdict with boundary conditions.
answer_options.C: Confirm feasibility, but add a 20% contingency to the timeline to cover unknown requirements.
answer_options.D: Decline to give a verdict until a full production build has been tested at real volume.

questions.explanation: Correct. A feasibility verdict is only as sound as the constraints gathered before it, and it must name its boundary conditions.

option_explanations.A: Capability isn't feasibility; unknown constraints can invalidate the design.
option_explanations.B: Correct. A feasibility verdict is only as sound as the constraints gathered before it, and it must name its boundary conditions.
option_explanations.C: Contingency doesn't replace missing constraints.
option_explanations.D: A verdict can be given at scoping time; it doesn't need a production build.

questions.exam_lesson: Collect volume, input size and latency before declaring feasibility.
questions.source_reference: M2 Sizing – "The scoping call that skipped the constraints"

questions.scenario: A wealth-management firm wants Claude to answer client questions about current portfolio values and recent trades, plus general questions about the firm's investment philosophy.
questions.question: Which property-driven design choice is most important?

answer_options.A: Fine-tune the model on the investment philosophy so its answers sound consistently on-brand.
answer_options.B: Enable extended thinking so the model recalls portfolio values and recent trades more accurately.
answer_options.C: Fetch portfolio values and trades by authorised tool calls; retrieve the philosophy content.
answer_options.D: Use the largest available context window and load every client's full portfolio history into it.

questions.explanation: Correct. The knowledge property means authoritative, changing data must come from the system of record via tools.

option_explanations.A: Fine-tuning is a late-stage option and doesn't address live values.
option_explanations.B: Thinking can't create facts the model doesn't have.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The knowledge property means authoritative, changing data must come from the system of record via tools.
option_explanations.D: Loading all histories inflates cost and exposes data; it's also stale.

questions.exam_lesson: Use the four properties to decide where an external system must be the source of truth.
questions.source_reference: M1 four properties (Knowledge); M1 retrieval vs. live state

questions.scenario: A scoping assessment for a document summariser finds it works for documents up to 150 pages but degrades beyond that because of context limits on the chosen tier. 8% of production documents exceed 150 pages.
questions.question: How should the feasibility verdict be stated?

answer_options.A: Feasible as scoped, because 92% of production documents fall within the supported length.
answer_options.B: Feasible with constraints: long documents need chunking or another tier; record it in the SOW.
answer_options.C: Not feasible, because some production documents exceed what the chosen tier can handle.
answer_options.D: Feasible as scoped, with a note to revisit long documents after launch if users report problems.

questions.explanation: Correct. The verdict plus the constraint that makes it true, documented so both teams know what's in scope.

option_explanations.A: Ignoring a known boundary turns into a production failure for 8% of traffic.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The verdict plus the constraint that makes it true, documented so both teams know what's in scope.
option_explanations.C: The limitation can be compensated (chunking or tier), so "not feasible" is wrong.
option_explanations.D: Deferring a known boundary means it goes undocumented, and an undocumented constraint fails in production.

questions.exam_lesson: "Feasible with constraints" means each constraint is documented and its failure mode named.
questions.source_reference: M2 Feasibility verdicts; M2 How to scope (boundary conditions)

questions.scenario: An invoice-extraction pipeline sends every document through OCR → extraction → ERP posting. Wrong extractions on unusual layouts get posted to the ERP at the same rate as clean ones.
questions.question: Which architectural element is missing?

answer_options.A: A larger, more capable model for the extraction step so unusual layouts are read correctly.
answer_options.B: Prompt caching for the extraction prompt so each document is processed faster and cheaper.
answer_options.C: A nightly batch job that re-runs every document through the pipeline to catch errors.
answer_options.D: Confidence scoring that routes low-confidence extractions to a human review queue first.

questions.explanation: Correct. Document pipelines fail most often through a missing exception path; confidence-based routing to a human queue is the mitigation.

option_explanations.A: A bigger model may help averages but doesn't stop wrong edge cases reaching the ERP.
option_explanations.B: Caching affects cost, not correctness.
option_explanations.C: Re-running repeats the same flow without an exception gate.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Document pipelines fail most often through a missing exception path; confidence-based routing to a human queue is the mitigation.

questions.exam_lesson: Every pipeline needs an exception path for low-confidence output.
questions.source_reference: M1 Reference architectures (document pipeline); M2 Failure modes

questions.scenario: A knowledge assistant's architecture diagram ends at "response returned to user". After launch, quality erodes for weeks before anyone notices.
questions.question: Which addition best completes the end-to-end design?

answer_options.A: Outcome signals feeding evals and a governance table with triggers, owners and actions.
answer_options.B: Higher-resolution latency dashboards with p50, p95 and p99 broken down by request type.
answer_options.C: A second model that reviews and rewrites every response before it's returned to the user.
answer_options.D: Monthly retraining of the model on recent user conversations so it keeps improving.

questions.explanation: Correct. A feedback loop of outcome signals, evals, triggers and owners is part of the architecture, not an add-on.

option_explanations.A: Correct. A feedback loop of outcome signals, evals, triggers and owners is part of the architecture, not an add-on.
option_explanations.B: Latency dashboards don't detect quality erosion.
option_explanations.C: Adds cost and latency without a detection mechanism.
option_explanations.D: Retraining isn't a standard lever here, and it doesn't replace detection and review.

questions.exam_lesson: Design input → processing → output → feedback loop; the loop is what detects degradation.
questions.source_reference: M2 Observability (outcome logging); M4 Feedback loop

questions.scenario: You are designing an end-to-end claims-summary system for adjusters. Inputs include claimant-submitted documents that may contain embedded instructions; outputs feed the claims system.
questions.question: Which TWO design elements belong at the input and output boundaries respectively? (Select 2)

answer_options.A: Input: screen submitted and retrieved content for injected instructions before it reaches the model, and inject identity server-side.
answer_options.B: Input: allow claimants to specify which adjuster role they want the summary written for.
answer_options.C: Output: validate against a schema and screen content before it is written to the claims system.
answer_options.D: Output: return free-form text so adjusters have maximum flexibility.
answer_options.E: Input: include every historical claim for the claimant in the prompt for context.

questions.explanation: Correct. Indirect injection arrives through submitted and retrieved content; identity must come from the server.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Indirect injection arrives through submitted and retrieved content; identity must come from the server.
option_explanations.B: Self-asserted role selection is an identity-spoofing path.
option_explanations.C: Correct. An output contract plus validation and screening protects the downstream system.
option_explanations.D: Free-form output breaks downstream integration and is harder to validate.
option_explanations.E: Over-loads context and over-exposes data; minimise to what the task needs.

questions.exam_lesson: Each stage of the end-to-end path has its own controls; input and output gates are different controls.
questions.source_reference: M3 Guardrails (indirect injection, output screening); M2 Identity, data minimisation

questions.scenario: Two months after launch, a reviewer-correction signal shows the extraction step is wrong on a new invoice layout that recently entered traffic.
questions.question: What should the feedback loop do?

answer_options.A: Silently raise the model tier for all documents so the new layout is handled better.
answer_options.B: Disable the pipeline until a full redesign is complete, to stop wrong extractions entirely.
answer_options.C: Add it to the golden set, diagnose the cause, then decide: iterate or re-architect.
answer_options.D: Ask reviewers to correct the new layout more carefully until the volume of errors drops.

questions.explanation: Correct. Signals → triage → decide → act → review, with the eval set kept current.

option_explanations.A: An unmeasured tier change hides the cause and inflates cost.
option_explanations.B: Overreaction; the loop should triage before deciding.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Signals → triage → decide → act → review, with the eval set kept current.
option_explanations.D: This shifts the burden to people and leaves the system unchanged.

questions.exam_lesson: Feedback signals should update evals and drive an explicit iterate-or-re-architect decision.
questions.source_reference: M4 Feedback loop; M2 Evals (keep dataset current)

questions.scenario: A team must classify incoming support emails into one of five known categories and send each to a dedicated handling chain. Classification is accurate in testing.
questions.question: Which pattern fits best?

answer_options.A: An autonomous agent that decides how to handle each email based on its content.
answer_options.B: A routing workflow: classify, then dispatch to a category-specific chain.
answer_options.C: A multi-agent system with one subagent per email, coordinated by an orchestrator.
answer_options.D: Fine-tune a separate model for each category and call the matching model per email.

questions.explanation: Correct. Routing suits distinct categories with accurate classification.

option_explanations.A: The categories and handlers are known; agent autonomy adds non-determinism with no benefit.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Routing suits distinct categories with accurate classification.
option_explanations.C: Multi-agent adds cost and failure boundaries without a reason.
option_explanations.D: Fine-tuning is a last step, not a pattern choice.

questions.exam_lesson: Known categories plus accurate classification means a routing workflow.
questions.source_reference: Official – Building effective agents (Routing); M1 Pattern selection

questions.scenario: A team built an agent for loan-disbursement approvals "to avoid constraining it". Months later, trace mining shows every run followed one of four paths, and an auditor asks which step approved a specific disbursement.
questions.question: What is the best redesign?

answer_options.A: Keep the agent and add more guardrail tools inside the loop to enforce each approval rule.
answer_options.B: Keep the agent but pin the model version so the auditor can see which version ran.
answer_options.C: Replace it with a larger model that explains its reasoning for each approval in the trace.
answer_options.D: Replace it with a router and four chains, giving discrete, auditable approval steps.

questions.explanation: Correct. When the paths are known, a workflow gives auditability and predictability.

option_explanations.A: That rebuilds the workflow inside the agent loop without the logging or auditability.
option_explanations.B: Pinning fixes a governance gap but not the missing auditable step.
option_explanations.C: Explanations aren't discrete, auditable control steps.
option_explanations.D: Correct. When the paths are known, a workflow gives auditability and predictability.

questions.exam_lesson: If the steps are knowable, write them in code.
questions.source_reference: M1 "When the team wanted flexibility and got non-determinism"

questions.scenario: An engineering org wants Claude to investigate unfamiliar legacy codebases and propose fixes for reported bugs. The investigation path depends on what each file reveals. Fixes can be reviewed before merge.
questions.question: Which pattern is most appropriate?

answer_options.A: An agent to investigate, then deterministic edit/test/review steps with review before merge.
answer_options.B: A fixed prompt chain that reads the same five core files for every bug, then proposes a fix.
answer_options.C: A single augmented call with the whole repository in context so nothing is missed.
answer_options.D: A routing workflow keyed on bug category, with one fix template for each category.

questions.explanation: Correct. Exploration is genuinely unpredictable (agentic), while edits follow deterministic steps with review; this is the coding-agent reference architecture.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Exploration is genuinely unpredictable (agentic), while edits follow deterministic steps with review; this is the coding-agent reference architecture.
option_explanations.B: A fixed chain can't adapt to what each codebase reveals.
option_explanations.C: Repositories exceed practical context; it's monolithic at its worst.
option_explanations.D: The investigation path depends on content, not a category label.

questions.exam_lesson: Use an agent where the path is unknowable, and deterministic steps where it isn't.
questions.source_reference: M1 Reference architectures (coding agent)

questions.scenario: A marketing team's copy generator has acceptable average quality but frequently misses brand-guideline rules. The rules are clear and checkable, and a second review pass measurably improves compliance in tests.
questions.question: Which pattern change is best justified?

answer_options.A: Fine-tune a model on past approved copy so it learns the brand guidelines implicitly.
answer_options.B: Switch to an autonomous agent with web search so it can look up brand guidance itself.
answer_options.C: Add few-shot examples of compliant copy to the prompt, without any separate checking step.
answer_options.D: An evaluator-optimizer workflow: generate, check against the criteria, refine.

questions.explanation: Correct. Evaluator-optimizer fits clear evaluation criteria where refinement gives measurable value.

option_explanations.A: Fine-tuning comes after prompt and pattern improvements; it also locks a model version.
option_explanations.B: More autonomy doesn't address rule compliance.
option_explanations.C: Examples may help, but checkable criteria plus measured gains from review point to an evaluator loop.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Evaluator-optimizer fits clear evaluation criteria where refinement gives measurable value.

questions.exam_lesson: Clear criteria plus measurable gains from refinement means evaluator-optimizer.
questions.source_reference: Official – Building effective agents (evaluator-optimizer); M1 Try prompting before fine-tuning

questions.scenario: A team says prompting "isn't reliable enough" for extracting fields from emails and proposes fine-tuning. They have not tried output schemas, examples, or a verification step.
questions.question: What is the recommended sequence?

answer_options.A: Fine-tune first for reliability, then add prompting improvements later on top of it.
answer_options.B: Prompt first, then tools or retrieval, then a stronger pattern; fine-tune last.
answer_options.C: Switch to an agent pattern so the model can check and correct its own extractions.
answer_options.D: Use the most capable model tier and skip evaluation, since capability solves reliability.

questions.explanation: Correct. Most reliability issues are prompt problems; fine-tuning is the last step in the progression.

option_explanations.A: Fine-tuning first locks you to a version and skips cheaper fixes.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Most reliability issues are prompt problems; fine-tuning is the last step in the progression.
option_explanations.C: An agent pattern adds non-determinism for a well-defined extraction.
option_explanations.D: Tier changes without evals are unjustified.

questions.exam_lesson: Prompt → tools/retrieval → stronger pattern → (rarely) fine-tune.
questions.source_reference: M1 Try prompting before you consider fine-tuning

questions.scenario: An orchestrator fans out a 50-section vendor-contract review to subagents and reports "48 sections reviewed, 3 flagged". Two subagents timed out or returned empty results.
questions.question: What design element would have prevented the misleading summary?

answer_options.A: A coverage check: results returned must equal units dispatched, else flag.
answer_options.B: A more capable model for the orchestrator so it writes a more accurate summary.
answer_options.C: Longer subagent timeouts so slow sections have more time to return their results.
answer_options.D: Running sections sequentially instead of in parallel so each result can be confirmed.

questions.explanation: Correct. Coverage must be verified; the orchestrator must reconcile counts and flag missing units.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Coverage must be verified; the orchestrator must reconcile counts and flag missing units.
option_explanations.B: Capability doesn't add a reconciliation rule.
option_explanations.C: Timeouts may still happen; nothing would notice them.
option_explanations.D: Sequential runs can drop units too, and lose the parallelism benefit.

questions.exam_lesson: Validate coverage; never assume it.
questions.source_reference: M1 "When fan-out hid a dropped unit"

questions.scenario: In a multi-agent due-diligence system, a long run fails when the orchestrator's process crashes after 70% of subagent work is complete, and everything restarts from zero.
questions.question: Which design response best addresses this?

answer_options.A: Give subagents larger context windows so each can finish its work in fewer turns.
answer_options.B: Merge all subagents into the orchestrator so there's only one process to keep alive.
answer_options.C: Checkpoint orchestrator state for resume; keep subagent work idempotent.
answer_options.D: Assign a human reviewer to monitor each run and restart it manually if it fails.

questions.explanation: Correct. Orchestrator failure is often unrecoverable unless its state is protected; idempotent subagents allow safe retries.

option_explanations.A: Subagent context doesn't protect orchestrator state.
option_explanations.B: That loses parallelism and clean contexts and doesn't add resumability.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Orchestrator failure is often unrecoverable unless its state is protected; idempotent subagents allow safe retries.
option_explanations.D: A human watching doesn't prevent lost state.

questions.exam_lesson: Protect the orchestrator; make subagent work retryable.
questions.source_reference: M1 Error recovery table

questions.scenario: Two subagents reviewing the same clause return conflicting verdicts (one "compliant", one "violation"). The orchestrator currently picks whichever result arrives first.
questions.question: What should the design specify?

answer_options.A: Always prefer the subagent whose explanation is longer and more detailed.
answer_options.B: An explicit conflict rule (stricter verdict wins, flagged) or human escalation.
answer_options.C: Run a third subagent and take the majority verdict, without recording the conflict.
answer_options.D: Drop conflicting units from the report so only agreed results are presented.

questions.explanation: Correct. How conflicts are resolved has to be designed: a defined rule or human escalation.

option_explanations.A: Explanation length isn't a correctness signal.
option_explanations.B: Correct. How conflicts are resolved has to be designed: a defined rule or human escalation.
option_explanations.C: Voting can be a valid technique, but silently resolving a high-stakes conflict without recording it hides risk.
option_explanations.D: Dropping units creates a silent coverage gap.

questions.exam_lesson: Decomposition, result structure and conflict resolution must all be designed explicitly.
questions.source_reference: M1 Multi-agent systems (three things must be designed); failure table

questions.scenario: A team proposes a multi-agent architecture for a task where each step depends heavily on the previous step's full context and the total material fits within one context window.
questions.question: What is the best recommendation?

answer_options.A: Proceed with multi-agent so the steps can run in parallel and finish sooner.
answer_options.B: Use one subagent per step so each works in a clean, focused context window.
answer_options.C: Use multi-agent, but share the full accumulated context with every agent.
answer_options.D: A single agent or workflow; multi-agent adds cost with no benefit here.

questions.explanation: Correct. Use multi-agent when work exceeds one context or parallelises; heavy dependencies are a poor fit.

option_explanations.A: Dependent steps can't parallelise meaningfully.
option_explanations.B: Splitting interdependent steps loses needed context.
option_explanations.C: Sharing full context with every agent multiplies tokens and defeats the purpose.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Use multi-agent when work exceeds one context or parallelises; heavy dependencies are a poor fit.

questions.exam_lesson: Use the fewest agents that meet the requirement.
questions.source_reference: M1 Multi-agent Cost·Complexity·Risk; Official – multi-agent research system

questions.scenario: You are designing an agentic finance-operations system where subagents can propose vendor payments and update ledger entries. Most actions are low-value ledger tags; a few are payments over $10,000.
questions.question: Which TWO human-in-the-loop design choices are most appropriate? (Select 2)

answer_options.A: A pre-action approval gate before any payment over the threshold.
answer_options.B: Pre-action approval for every ledger tag, so nothing at all goes through unreviewed.
answer_options.C: Sampled review of low-value, reversible ledger tags.
answer_options.D: Post-action audit for large payments, since throughput matters.
answer_options.E: No human checkpoints; rely on the orchestrator's synthesis.

questions.explanation: Correct. Gate irreversible or high-stakes actions before they happen.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Gate irreversible or high-stakes actions before they happen.
option_explanations.B: Gating everything causes consent fatigue and degrades review.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Sample lower-stakes actions instead of gating each one.
option_explanations.D: A post-action audit comes too late for hard-to-reverse payments.
option_explanations.E: The orchestrator isn't an approval control.

questions.exam_lesson: Checkpoint placement is part of orchestration design: gate high-stakes actions, sample low-stakes ones.
questions.source_reference: M1 HITL checkpoint patterns; M3 Review routing

questions.scenario: For each part of a request, an architect must decide whether Claude, an existing system, or a human should own it.
questions.question: Which criteria does the module give for justifying each delegation?

answer_options.A: Speed, cost and the size of the model involved.
answer_options.B: Reversibility, stakes and accountability.
answer_options.C: Volume, latency and token count.
answer_options.D: Accuracy, fluency and tone.

questions.explanation: Correct. Can a wrong call be undone? What does it cost? Who must answer for it?

option_explanations.A: These matter elsewhere, but they aren't the delegation criteria.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Can a wrong call be undone? What does it cost? Who must answer for it?
option_explanations.C: These are sizing inputs, not ownership criteria.
option_explanations.D: These are output qualities.

questions.exam_lesson: Delegation is justified by reversibility, stakes and accountability.
questions.source_reference: M1 Decomposition – Delegation

questions.scenario: A report-generation task has three independent sections (market, competitors, regulation) and a final executive summary that depends on all three.
questions.question: Which decomposition is best?

answer_options.A: Generate all four parts in parallel to minimise total latency.
answer_options.B: One agent writes the full report in a single pass to keep it coherent.
answer_options.C: Parallelise the three sections, then a gated synthesis step for the summary.
answer_options.D: Chain all four parts sequentially, each step consuming the last, without checks.

questions.explanation: Correct. Parallelise only independent units, then synthesise, with gates between stages.

option_explanations.A: The summary depends on the sections, so it can't run in parallel with them.
option_explanations.B: Misses parallelism and checks, and the context can grow large.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Parallelise only independent units, then synthesise, with gates between stages.
option_explanations.D: Sequential work wastes the parallel opportunity and has no gates.

questions.exam_lesson: Only independent units go in parallel; put a gate before dependent steps.
questions.source_reference: Official – Building effective agents (parallelization, prompt chaining gates); M1 Fan-out

questions.scenario: A contracts team must process 300-page framework agreements on a tier whose context window can't hold the whole document plus instructions comfortably.
questions.question: Which decomposition approach is most appropriate?

answer_options.A: Truncate each agreement to its first 100 pages, where most key terms usually appear.
answer_options.B: Summarise the whole document in one call, then run the analysis on the summary.
answer_options.C: Use monolithic context with the full document and accept truncation at the window limit.
answer_options.D: Split by section, extract against a schema, then synthesise with a coverage check.

questions.explanation: Correct. Inputs exceeding the window need a pipeline or chunked decomposition; alternatively the tier's window becomes part of the model decision.

option_explanations.A: Truncation silently drops required content.
option_explanations.B: The first call still can't hold the document, and the summary drops load-bearing detail.
option_explanations.C: Truncation is a silent failure.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Inputs exceeding the window need a pipeline or chunked decomposition; alternatively the tier's window becomes part of the model decision.

questions.exam_lesson: When inputs exceed working memory, decompose the input itself.
questions.source_reference: M2 Feasibility – working memory; M2 scoping case (context window per tier)

questions.scenario: A deployment lets compliance review 100% of trader communications instead of a 5% sample, which wasn't previously possible.
questions.question: Which business value pillar does this primarily represent?

answer_options.A: Efficiency
answer_options.B: Transformation
answer_options.C: Cost
answer_options.D: Performance SLA

questions.explanation: Correct. Transformation means work that wasn't feasible before becomes possible.

option_explanations.A: Efficiency means the same work done faster or cheaper; here new work becomes possible.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Transformation means work that wasn't feasible before becomes possible.
option_explanations.C: Cost refers to the solution's run cost.
option_explanations.D: SLAs are service levels the deployment must hold.

questions.exam_lesson: Tag each value claim with its pillar.
questions.source_reference: M2 Business value and ROI mapping (five pillars); EG Domain 1

questions.scenario: A business case projects analyst hours falling from 40 to 0 per week. The design routes low-confidence outputs (about 20%) to analyst review.
questions.question: What is wrong with the ROI projection?

answer_options.A: It assumes full automation although analysts still review 20% of outputs.
answer_options.B: It should measure model accuracy rather than analyst hours to show the benefit.
answer_options.C: It should report tokens saved rather than hours, since tokens drive cost.
answer_options.D: Nothing; review time belongs in the build cost, not in the projection.

questions.explanation: Correct. Where the design includes HITL review, the projected state must include that labour.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Where the design includes HITL review, the projected state must include that labour.
option_explanations.B: The business unit (hours) is right; accuracy isn't the value unit.
option_explanations.C: Tokens aren't a business metric for the sponsor.
option_explanations.D: Review is a recurring operational cost, not a build cost.

questions.exam_lesson: Net human-review effort out of projected gains.
questions.source_reference: M2 ROI mapping Step 2; ROI risks table

questions.scenario: A sponsor takes an outcome document to the CFO. It lists 40,000 requests a month, 1.8 s average latency and a 0.4% error rate. The CFO asks what the deployment changed for the business.
questions.question: Which fields should the document have included?

answer_options.A: p95 latency, per-request token counts and the cache hit rate.
answer_options.B: The model tier and context strategy used at each pipeline step.
answer_options.C: Before/after business metric, an auditable control, an owner.
answer_options.D: The prompts used, so the CFO can see how the system works.

questions.explanation: Correct. Before/after on the targeted business metric, plus an auditable control and an owner, is what justifies expansion.

option_explanations.A: These are still technical metrics.
option_explanations.B: These are architecture details, not business outcomes.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Before/after on the targeted business metric, plus an auditable control and an owner, is what justifies expansion.
option_explanations.D: Prompts don't show business value.

questions.exam_lesson: Technical metrics show it runs; before/after business metrics show it's worth expanding.
questions.source_reference: M4 "The outcome document that measured the wrong thing"; template

questions.scenario: A projected payback period of 4 months was computed using the average token cost per request. Sizing shows a heavy-tailed distribution where 10% of requests consume most tokens, and volume could be 40% lower than forecast.
questions.question: How should the architect present the business case?

answer_options.A: Present the 4-month payback as the plan, since it was calculated from real averages.
answer_options.B: Remove the long-document requests from the analysis because they're atypical.
answer_options.C: Present only the best-case figure to secure funding, and revise it after launch.
answer_options.D: Recompute run cost from the distribution and give payback with sensitivity.

option_explanations.B: Correct. Thinking is a cost/latency trade-off justified only by a measured accuracy gap; here there's none.

questions.explanation: Correct. LLMs fail by producing subtly wrong output; log downstream outcomes and compare output distributions over time.

questions.scenario: After a quality drop, the team can't tell whether it came from a model version roll-forward, a shift in customer query topics, or the model behaving differently on unchanged inputs. Logs record only input and output text.
questions.question: Which instrumentation would best enable correct change attribution?

answer_options.A: Log model version and prompt ID, pin versions, compare outputs on stable inputs.
answer_options.B: Increase log retention to two years so earlier behaviour can be compared with today's.
answer_options.C: Add a thumbs-up/down button so users can report which answers have become worse.
answer_options.D: Log the full retrieved context for every request in plaintext so engineers can replay it.

questions.explanation: Correct. Version and prompt identifiers plus pinning separate model-update effects; topic distributions show data drift; stable-input comparison shows model drift.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Version and prompt identifiers plus pinning separate model-update effects; topic distributions show data drift; stable-input comparison shows model drift.
option_explanations.B: Retention doesn't add the fields needed for attribution.
option_explanations.C: Feedback signals a problem but doesn't attribute its cause.
option_explanations.D: Context logs can help debugging, but without version metadata and drift comparison you still can't attribute, and plaintext adds data-handling risk.

questions.scenario: A security organisation will approve an autonomous IT-operations agent only if the architect demonstrates adequate observability across the surfaces the agent uses.

answer_options.A: Verify which agentic actions each surface records in audit logs, and close any unlogged action paths.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer builds RAG over 20,000 equipment manuals. Technicians search mostly by part number and fault code, sometimes with free-text descriptions.
questions.question: Which indexing strategy best fits?

answer_options.A: Dense embeddings only, because semantic search handles part numbers and free text alike.

answer_options.D: No index; put the most relevant manuals in a monolithic prompt and rely on prompt caching.

option_explanations.B: Correct. Mixed patterns (exact codes plus free text) are the classic hybrid case; RRF is the standard low-tuning fusion.

questions.scenario: A RAG system over insurance policies uses fixed 500-token chunks. Answers often cite an exclusion clause without the section heading that says it applies only to commercial policies.
questions.question: What chunking change most directly fixes this?

answer_options.A: Switch to hierarchical chunking that keeps each clause with its section and subsection context.
answer_options.B: Reduce chunk size to 200 tokens so each clause is retrieved more precisely on its own.
answer_options.C: Increase top-k from 5 to 20 so the heading is more likely to be retrieved alongside the clause.
answer_options.D: Replace the embedding model with a larger one that understands policy language better.

questions.explanation: Correct. In structured documents, section context carries meaning; hierarchical chunking keeps it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. In structured documents, section context carries meaning; hierarchical chunking keeps it.
option_explanations.B: Smaller fixed chunks separate the clause from its heading even more.

questions.scenario: After the weekly document refresh, a policy RAG system starts returning confident but outdated answers. Model version and latency are unchanged. Investigation shows new documents were embedded with a newer embedding model while the query encoder still uses the old one.
questions.question: What is the correct remediation?

answer_options.A: Lower the model temperature so the model is less confident when it's unsure of the answer.
answer_options.B: Add an instruction telling the model to prefer the newest documents when sources conflict.
answer_options.C: Upgrade the generation model to a more capable tier that can detect outdated content.
answer_options.D: Re-index with one embedding model for documents and queries; add retrieval checks.

questions.explanation: Correct. Mismatched embeddings break similarity; re-index consistently and keep retrieval quality in the eval loop.

option_explanations.A: Temperature doesn't fix mismatched embeddings feeding wrong context.
option_explanations.B: The model can't prefer documents that retrieval never surfaces.
option_explanations.C: Generation quality isn't the cause; retrieval feeds poor context.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mismatched embeddings break similarity; re-index consistently and keep retrieval quality in the eval loop.

questions.scenario: A team's RAG pipeline was well-tuned at launch. Six months later the corpus has tripled and answer quality has slowly declined, though no code changed.
questions.question: What practice would have caught this earliest?

answer_options.B: Running monthly load tests on the API to confirm throughput and latency stay within SLA.
answer_options.C: Pinning the generation model version so behaviour can't change without a deployment.

option_explanations.B: Load tests measure throughput and latency, not retrieval relevance.
option_explanations.C: Pinning helps attribution but nothing changed in the model here.

questions.scenario: A retailer's assistant answers "Where is my order?" from a vector index refreshed nightly from order-status exports. Customers receive confident but outdated statuses.

answer_options.D: Use a better embedding model trained on logistics text so order chunks match queries closely.

option_explanations.B: Similarity isn't truth; a highly similar stale snapshot is still stale.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Live state belongs to the system of record and is fetched via a tool call; stable FAQ content suits retrieval.

questions.scenario: A bank's assistant must answer questions about fee policies (a 40-page document updated quarterly) and about each customer's current account balance.

answer_options.A: Index both the fee policy and nightly balance snapshots in the same vector store.
answer_options.B: Policy via RAG or a cached prefix; balances via an authorised core-banking tool call.

answer_options.D: Put both the fee policy and the customer's full transaction history in every prompt.

option_explanations.A: Balances are live state; snapshots will be wrong and give no error signal.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Stable policy suits retrieval or a cached prefix; balances are live state owned by the core system and must be fetched with authorization.

option_explanations.D: Monolithic loading inflates cost and over-exposes data.

questions.scenario: A pharma research assistant must answer questions that require synthesising findings across 30 related trial reports. The current top-5 RAG returns fragments that each look relevant but the answers miss cross-report patterns.
questions.question: Which approach best addresses the limitation?

answer_options.A: Raise top-k to 50 so more relevant fragments reach the model, and let it synthesise across them.

questions.explanation: Correct. When synthesis needs many documents scored independently, per-unit extraction plus structured synthesis fits better than top-k chunks.

questions.scenario: A team plans to test a new prompt. Their hypothesis reads: "The new prompt is better."

answer_options.A: It is too long to state in the experiment-tracking tool that the team uses.
answer_options.B: It should be phrased negatively, as a null hypothesis, before it can be tested.
answer_options.C: It names no treatment, metric or threshold, so any result can be read as a win.
answer_options.D: Prompts can't be A/B tested; only model versions can be compared that way.

questions.explanation: Correct. A usable hypothesis names the treatment, the primary metric's expected direction, the threshold and any secondary constraints.

option_explanations.B: Wording style isn't the problem the course identifies.

questions.scenario: A test of a new prompt shows task success rising from 70% to 73% at statistical significance, but cost per completion rises 30% and the budget is tight.
questions.question: How should the result be read?

answer_options.A: Ship it immediately, because the improvement is statistically significant.
answer_options.B: Rerun the test with a smaller sample until the cost difference disappears.
answer_options.C: Ignore cost, because the primary metric was task success and it went up.
answer_options.D: Weigh the gain against the cost before deciding.

questions.explanation: Correct. Ask whether the effect is large enough to justify the overhead, and whether any secondary metric degraded.

option_explanations.A: Significance says the effect is probably real, not that it's worth shipping.
option_explanations.B: Shrinking the sample to change the result is outcome shopping.
option_explanations.C: Secondary metrics that degrade must be considered before declaring a winner.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Ask whether the effect is large enough to justify the overhead, and whether any secondary metric degraded.

questions.scenario: A regulated claims system wants to validate a new model version against real traffic, but exposing any customer to an unvalidated change isn't permitted.
questions.question: Which approach fits?

answer_options.A: Shadow testing, scored offline while users get the current version.
answer_options.B: A live A/B test with a very small treatment group, such as 1% of traffic.
answer_options.C: Switch everyone to the new version over a weekend, when traffic is lowest.
answer_options.D: Skip validation, since the model provider tests new versions before release.

questions.explanation: Correct. Shadow testing decides before any user sees the new version; it is often the only acceptable option in regulated settings.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Shadow testing decides before any user sees the new version; it is often the only acceptable option in regulated settings.
option_explanations.B: Even a small live split exposes real users to an unvalidated change.
option_explanations.C: That exposes everyone, with no measurement.
option_explanations.D: A model change is a release; the partner must validate it against its own workload.

questions.exam_lesson: Use shadow testing when one bad output is too risky or a live split isn't allowed.
questions.source_reference: M2 Shadow testing

questions.scenario: A prompt change passed a two-week A/B test during a quiet period. A seasonal spike then brought a surge of unusual claim types, and performance on those dropped sharply.

answer_options.A: The test used too many users, which diluted the effect of the treatment.

option_explanations.B: Correct. A change can help typical inputs and hurt rare ones, so align the test period and input distribution with real traffic.
option_explanations.C: Nothing in the scenario points to stopping early.

questions.scenario: A sponsor's KPI dashboard tracks average handle time and first-contact resolution. The engineering dashboard tracks latency, task success and error rate. At the business review nobody can explain why handle time moved.
questions.question: What should have been built at design time?

answer_options.A: A separate engineering dashboard for each business unit that uses the assistant.
answer_options.B: A higher sampling rate on the request traces collected by the observability stack.
answer_options.C: A translation layer from technical metrics to the sponsor's KPIs.
answer_options.D: A monthly written report summarising every alert that fired during the period.

questions.explanation: Correct. The translation layer connects technical metrics to the business metrics they drive, so it can be queried live.

option_explanations.A: More dashboards don't connect technical and business metrics.
option_explanations.B: More sampling of technical data still doesn't speak the sponsor's language.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The translation layer connects technical metrics to the business metrics they drive, so it can be queried live.
option_explanations.D: A retrospective report is the reconstruction the translation layer is meant to avoid.

questions.scenario: A deployment's aggregate cost per request looks normal, but the monthly bill keeps exceeding forecasts.

answer_options.A: A higher-level dashboard that rolls all metrics into one health score.
answer_options.B: Per-request decomposition of cost and tokens to expose the heavy tail.
answer_options.C: An alert that fires whenever the error rate rises above zero.
answer_options.D: A weekly summary email sent to engineering leads with the top metrics.

questions.explanation: Correct. Aggregate metrics can look healthy while a small fraction of requests consumes most of the budget.

option_explanations.A: More aggregation hides the tail further.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Aggregate metrics can look healthy while a small fraction of requests consumes most of the budget.
option_explanations.C: Error rate isn't the issue here.
option_explanations.D: A summary of aggregates repeats the same blind spot.

questions.scenario: Over eight weeks a deployment's eval score drifted down steadily. The error rate stayed flat, so no alert fired, and the next scheduled review is a quarter away.
questions.question: What should the monitoring design include?

answer_options.A: A quality-drift trigger mapped to an owner and an action in the governance table.
answer_options.B: A tighter error-rate alert threshold, so smaller error spikes are reported sooner.
answer_options.C: More frequent quarterly reviews of the full dashboard by the engineering team.
answer_options.D: A larger eval dataset, scored at the next quarterly review against the baseline.

questions.explanation: Correct. Monitoring needs a decision layer: slow drifts, not just hard failures, map to triggers, owners and actions.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Monitoring needs a decision layer: slow drifts, not just hard failures, map to triggers, owners and actions.
option_explanations.B: The error rate didn't move, so a tighter threshold still wouldn't fire.
option_explanations.C: Scheduled reviews are what let the drift run for weeks.
option_explanations.D: Better measurement scored too late still catches it too late.

questions.source_reference: M4 The observability stack that replaced the feedback loop; M5 The drift that waited for a quarterly review

questions.scenario: A team sets up anomaly alerts for a new deployment and asks which thresholds the course gives as examples.
questions.question: Which pair matches the course's examples?

questions.explanation: Correct. Module two gives these two examples, and notes that model drift needs periodic distribution comparison instead.

option_explanations.D: These are product metrics, not the course's anomaly examples.

questions.exam_lesson: Alert on cost spikes against a baseline and on p95 crossing the SLA; compare distributions for drift.

questions.scenario: An internal assistant refused every harmful prompt in testing, so the team assumed it would also refuse requests for another business unit's records. In production it returned such a record for an ordinary-looking request.
questions.question: What was the design mistake?

answer_options.A: The model's safety training should have been tuned more strictly for this partner.

answer_options.C: A domain rule was left to trained alignment and enforced nowhere.
answer_options.D: The team should have used a larger model with stronger built-in safety behaviour.

questions.explanation: Correct. Claude can't enforce a rule it was never given; deployment rules need application-layer enforcement.

option_explanations.A: Trained alignment is general by design and can't know a partner's domain policy.
option_explanations.B: The request wasn't toxic; screening for harmful content doesn't enforce data access rules.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Claude can't enforce a rule it was never given; deployment rules need application-layer enforcement.
option_explanations.D: No model tier knows your authorisation model.

questions.exam_lesson: Training reduces broad harm; your domain policy must live in a layer you build.

questions.scenario: A RAG assistant screens every user message for prompt injection. An attacker plants instructions in a document that later gets indexed, and the model follows them.
questions.question: Which control was missing?

answer_options.A: A stronger user-input classifier, tuned to catch more of the known jailbreak phrases.
answer_options.B: Screening retrieved content and tool outputs before they are added to the model's context.
answer_options.C: A rule that users may only ask questions about documents they uploaded themselves.
answer_options.D: A longer system prompt that tells the model to ignore any instructions found in documents.

questions.explanation: Correct. Indirect injection arrives through retrieved content or tool outputs and needs its own screening.

option_explanations.A: The malicious text never passed through user input, so input screening can't see it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Indirect injection arrives through retrieved content or tool outputs and needs its own screening.
option_explanations.C: Document ownership doesn't stop planted instructions in shared corpora.
option_explanations.D: Instructions aren't enforcement and can be overridden.

questions.exam_lesson: Screen retrieved content and tool outputs, not just user input; indirect injection is the dominant vector.
questions.source_reference: M3 A second injection vector

questions.scenario: The team's own output-screening service starts timing out under peak load. The calling code currently lets responses through unscreened when the service errors.
questions.question: What should the architect change?

answer_options.A: Make it fail closed and log every failed gate.

answer_options.C: Remove output screening, because Anthropic's built-in controls already cover it.

questions.explanation: Correct. An operator-built guardrail that fails open gives the appearance of protection with none of the function.

option_explanations.A: Correct. An operator-built guardrail that fails open gives the appearance of protection with none of the function.
option_explanations.B: That silently drops protection when it's most likely to be tested.
option_explanations.C: Built-in controls don't enforce the partner's domain policy.
option_explanations.D: Long timeouts degrade latency and still leave the failure direction undefined.

questions.source_reference: M3 Fail open versus fail closed

questions.scenario: A team wants to install a third-party Skill that claims to "format reports". On inspection, its bundle reads environment variables and makes an outbound network request.
questions.question: What is the right action?

answer_options.A: Install it, since the platform screens Skills automatically before they run.
answer_options.B: Install it, but rely on output screening to catch anything unusual afterwards.
answer_options.C: Record a reject or remediate verdict: the behaviour is out of scope for a formatter.
answer_options.D: Install it once, observe its behaviour in production, then decide whether to keep it.

questions.explanation: Correct. Audit against the stated purpose; credential reads and network calls are findings. Then reject, or remediate and re-audit, and run approved Skills sandboxed with least privilege.

option_explanations.A: Don't assume the platform screens Skills; verify what vetting exists.
option_explanations.B: By the time output screening sees anything, the code has already run.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Audit against the stated purpose; credential reads and network calls are findings. Then reject, or remediate and re-audit, and run approved Skills sandboxed with least privilege.
option_explanations.D: Testing an untrusted bundle in production is the risk the audit exists to avoid.

questions.exam_lesson: Audit Skills before trust, record a verdict, confine them at runtime, and prefer trusted sources.

questions.scenario: Users of a public chatbot paste enormous blocks of padding text, which fill the context window, truncate answers and inflate cost.

option_explanations.A: Indirect injection arrives through retrieved content or tool outputs, not direct user padding.
option_explanations.B: The harm here is budget and truncation, not sensitive data leaking.
option_explanations.C: Tool abuse is about side-effecting tools called outside policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Oversized or padded inputs that consume the context or output budget are token-budget exhaustion.

questions.scenario: A security reviewer asks the architect for the risk assessment of a new Claude system. The architect offers to walk the reviewer through the design verbally.

questions.scenario: A financial reconciliation pipeline ran perfectly in five demo runs. In week two of production, the same statement re-processed produced a different categorisation, found only by chance.

answer_options.A: Non-determinism; outputs should have been verified rather than trusted as repeatable.

questions.explanation: Correct. A demo isn't evidence of determinism; the architecture needed checks around model output.

option_explanations.B: Nothing suggests truncation; the same input gave different outputs.
option_explanations.C: The issue is variability, not missing knowledge.
option_explanations.D: Prompt detail doesn't make a non-deterministic system deterministic.

questions.scenario: A benefits system makes eligibility decisions. Some are low-confidence and would remove a person's benefits if wrong; others are confident and easily reversed.

answer_options.A: Route every decision to a human reviewer, so that nothing goes through unchecked.

answer_options.D: Route only decisions the model labels as uncertain, whatever their cost or reversibility.

questions.explanation: Correct. Cost and reversibility set the stakes; calibrated confidence decides how much of that volume needs review.

option_explanations.C: Correct. Cost and reversibility set the stakes; calibrated confidence decides how much of that volume needs review.
option_explanations.D: Confidence alone ignores the consequences of a mistake.

questions.scenario: Reviewers see only the model's output and an approve button. They approve about 400 items a day, and quality problems are slipping through.

questions.explanation: Correct. Without inputs and the flag reason, a reviewer can't tell an edge case from routine traffic. Pair this with routing by stakes to cut the volume.
